subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Coarctation of the aorta and persistent pulmonary hypertension
vignette: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for headaches and an elevated blood pressure of 165/95 mm Hg measured in his right arm. His femoral pulses are weak and delayed relative to the radial pulse. Chest x-ray shows notching of the inferior surfaces of several posterior ribs.
question: Which of the following best explains the rib notching seen on this patient's chest x-ray?

options.text: Direct erosion of the ribs by the narrowed segment of the descending aorta
Enlarged intercostal arteries serving as collateral circulation around the aortic narrowing
Dilation of the bronchial arteries supplying the posterior chest wall
Calcification and tortuosity of the internal thoracic (mammary) arteries
Pulsatile expansion of berry aneurysms in the posterior intercostal arteries

explanation_correct: This patient has coarctation of the aorta, an aortic narrowing near the insertion of the ductus arteriosus ('juxtaductal'), causing upper-extremity hypertension and weak, delayed lower-extremity pulses (brachiofemoral delay). With age, the intercostal arteries enlarge due to collateral circulation around the narrowing, which produces rib-notching on x-ray. Coarctation is associated with bicuspid aortic valve and Turner syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: The coarcted aortic segment lies medial to the ribs and does not itself erode them; the notching is from enlarged intercostal vessels running along the inferior rib surfaces.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bronchial artery dilation is not the described collateral pathway in coarctation; intercostal arteries enlarge and groove the ribs.
explanation_incorrect.D: Internal thoracic artery calcification and tortuosity would not notch the ribs; the notching is caused by enlarged intercostal arteries.
explanation_incorrect.E: Berry aneurysms occur in the cerebral circulation (and are an associated complication of coarctation), not in the intercostal arteries.

educationalObjective: In coarctation of the aorta, enlarged intercostal arteries from collateral circulation produce inferior rib notching on chest x-ray.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Coarctation of the aorta and persistent pulmonary hypertension
vignette: A 19-year-old woman with Turner syndrome and known juxtaductal coarctation of the aorta presents with the abrupt onset of the worst headache of her life followed by vomiting and neck stiffness. CT shows diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage. Her arm blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg, and her femoral pulses are weak and delayed.
question: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her intracranial hemorrhage?

options.text: Rupture of a berry aneurysm of the cerebral circulation
Rupture of the coarctated segment of the descending thoracic aorta
Hemorrhagic transformation of an infective endocarditis-related embolic infarct
Rupture of an enlarged intercostal collateral artery into the spinal canal
Intraparenchymal bleed from severe chronic systemic hypertension alone

explanation_correct: Coarctation of the aorta increases the risk of cerebral hemorrhage from berry aneurysms, which present exactly as seen here — sudden severe headache with subarachnoid hemorrhage. Turner syndrome is associated with coarctation and bicuspid aortic valve, and other complications of coarctation include heart failure, aortic rupture, and infective endocarditis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Aortic rupture is a recognized complication of coarctation, but it presents with chest/back pain and cardiovascular collapse rather than isolated subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanation_incorrect.C: Infective endocarditis is a complication of coarctation, but the classic cause of sudden subarachnoid hemorrhage in this setting is a berry aneurysm, not an embolic infarct with hemorrhagic transformation.
explanation_incorrect.D: Enlarged intercostal collaterals cause rib notching but do not rupture into the spinal canal to produce subarachnoid hemorrhage.
explanation_incorrect.E: Chronic hypertension can cause intraparenchymal hemorrhage in typical locations (basal ganglia, thalamus), but the sudden 'worst headache of my life' with diffuse SAH points to berry aneurysm rupture.

educationalObjective: Complications of coarctation of the aorta include HF, cerebral hemorrhage from berry aneurysms, aortic rupture, and infective endocarditis.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Coarctation of the aorta and persistent pulmonary hypertension
vignette: A term newborn develops severe respiratory distress with tachypnea and diffuse cyanosis several hours after delivery complicated by meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Oxygen saturation measured in the right arm (preductal) is 88%, while saturation measured in the leg (postductal) is 72%. Pulses are equal in the upper and lower extremities.
question: Which of the following best explains the difference between the preductal and postductal saturations in this newborn?

options.text: Right-to-left shunting through the ductus arteriosus delivering relatively desaturated blood to the descending aorta while high pulmonary vascular resistance persists
Narrowing of the aorta distal to the ductus limiting oxygenated blood delivery to the lower body
Transposed great vessels creating parallel circulations with aorta-to-pulmonary-artery mixing through the ductus
A left-to-right ductal shunt diluting the descending aorta with venous blood
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return diverting oxygenated blood away from the systemic circulation

explanation_correct: This newborn has persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), in which high pulmonary vascular resistance persists after birth — risk factors include aspiration of meconium-stained amniotic fluid and neonatal pneumonia. It leads to right-to-left shunting through the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, so preductal O2 saturation is often greater than postductal, with signs of respiratory distress, often differential cyanosis, and equal pulses (no delay).

explanation_incorrect.B: Coarctation is an anatomic narrowing of the aorta; it causes brachiofemoral pulse delay, whereas this newborn has equal pulses, and the preductal/postductal saturation gradient in PPHN reflects active right-to-left ductal shunting.
explanation_incorrect.C: D-transposition creates separate parallel circulations and profound early cyanosis, but the preductal > postductal saturation gradient with equal pulses and meconium aspiration points to PPHN.
explanation_incorrect.D: A left-to-right ductal shunt delivers oxygenated aortic blood to the pulmonary artery and would not lower postductal saturations; the postductal desaturation here requires right-to-left ductal flow.
explanation_incorrect.E: TAPVR drains pulmonary veins into the right heart and requires an ASD for survival, producing uniform cyanosis rather than a preductal/postductal saturation difference with equal pulses.

educationalObjective: In PPHN, persistent high pulmonary vascular resistance causes right-to-left shunting through the foramen ovale and ductus, so preductal saturation exceeds postductal saturation with equal pulses.

subject: Cardiovascular
subtopic: Coarctation of the aorta and persistent pulmonary hypertension
vignette: A newborn has respiratory distress with tachypnea and differential cyanosis; the preductal oxygen saturation (right arm) is higher than the postductal saturation (leg). The pediatrician notes that the femoral pulses feel equal in timing and volume to the brachial pulses.
question: Which of the following best explains why equal pulses in this newborn help distinguish persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn from postductal coarctation of the aorta?

options.text: PPHN causes hypertension in the upper extremities with weak delayed lower-extremity pulses
In PPHN the ductus delivers mixed blood to the descending aorta without mechanical obstruction of aortic flow, so there is no brachiofemoral delay
In PPHN the ductal shunt is left to right, augmenting femoral pulse volume above brachial levels
In PPHN the foramen ovale shunt selectively reduces flow to the subclavian arteries
In PPHN equal pulses indicate that the ductus arteriosus has already closed completely

explanation_correct: PPHN produces differential cyanosis and a preductal > postductal saturation gradient through right-to-left shunting across the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, but because flow to the descending aorta is not mechanically obstructed, pulses are equal (no delay). Postductal coarctation, by contrast, physically narrows the aorta and produces weak, delayed lower-extremity pulses (brachiofemoral delay).

explanation_incorrect.A: Upper-extremity hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses is the signature of coarctation of the aorta, not of PPHN, which characteristically has equal pulses.
explanation_incorrect.C: The ductal shunt in PPHN is right to left (desaturated venous blood into the descending aorta); it does not augment femoral pulse volume.
explanation_incorrect.D: The foramen ovale shunt in PPHN delivers venous blood to the left atrium and systemic circulation generally; it does not selectively reduce subclavian flow or explain pulse timing.
explanation_incorrect.E: Equal pulses occur despite the open ductus, because there is no anatomic obstruction; a closed ductus in PPHN would eliminate the postductal desaturation rather than cause it.

educationalObjective: PPHN causes differential cyanosis with equal pulses (no brachiofemoral delay), which distinguishes it from coarctation of the aorta.
